answer: The paper's ITL formula ITL = alpha/(1-lambda*W) captures the correct direction but the wrong shape. Over rates 1-150 req/s it fits with R²=0.939 (AL) and R²=0.960 (AD) — adequate but structurally biased. The paper predicts a convex (accelerating) curve, but BLIS produces a concave (saturating) curve. A corrected 3-parameter model ITL = a + b*rate/(1+d*rate) fits with R²=0.997 (AL) and R²=0.9985 (AD) across 120 simulations (12 rates x 2 modes x 5 seeds), with mean absolute error 11x smaller than the paper's model. The paper model's residuals follow an S-shaped pattern: overshoots at low rates (0.3-0.8ms), undershoots at mid-rates (0.6-1.1ms), overshoots again near rate=150. This S-shape is unfixable — no parameter choice can make the convex alpha/(1-rho) match concave data. The mechanism: BLIS's step-time formula has fixed per-step costs (weight loading beta3*tWeight=1284us, beta7=126us) that are amortized over the batch. As rate increases, batch size grows and per-token overhead drops — a concave relationship the paper's constant-alpha assumption misses. At rate=1 (batch size=1), AL and AD produce identical ITL=12.260953ms (confirmed across 5 seeds to 9 decimal places), proving the amortization mechanism is absent when there is no batching. AD consistently yields lower ITL than AL (by 0.06ms at rate=5 to 1.69ms at rate=150) because dedicated prefill instances reduce decode-side utilization. AD incurs 4.2-15.7ms higher TTFT due to KV transfer (~3.4ms at 25 GB/s) plus prefill queueing, but is E2E-superior at all rates (benefit: 29-255ms) because the ITL savings over 127 decode tokens dominate the TTFT penalty.
